opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's a bit of a paradox, right? It's what people sometimes call Moravec's paradox. Things we find hard as humans, like playing chess or passing the bar exam or writing code, turn out to be relatively easy for computers. Things that any cat or a ten-month-old baby can do, like understanding that an object falls when you let go of it, or planning how to jump onto a shelf, are incredibly hard for AI systems.

Language is easier than we thought because it's discrete. There's a finite number of tokens in a vocabulary, maybe 30,000 to 100,000. So when you train a system to predict the next word, it can never predict exactly which word comes next, but it can produce a probability distribution over all possible words, and that's a tractable thing to represent. Language is also, in a sense, already a compressed, abstract representation of the world. Humans have done a lot of the work.

The physical world is nothing like that. It's high-dimensional, continuous, and noisy. If you try to train a system to predict what happens next in a video at the pixel level, you basically can't do it. There's an infinite number of plausible futures, and you don't know how to represent a distribution over all possible video frames. Most of the details are fundamentally unpredictable anyway, like the exact position of every leaf on a tree moving in the wind. So a system trained to predict pixels wastes all its capacity trying to predict things that can't be predicted, and you end up with blurry predictions and no real understanding.

There's also a data argument. A typical large language model is trained on something like 10^13 or more tokens, which would take a human hundreds of thousands of years to read. But a four-year-old child has been awake for roughly 16,000 hours, and the amount of data that's gone through their optic nerve is on the same order of magnitude, maybe more. So in four years a child has seen as much data as the biggest LLMs, but through vision and touch, not text. And from that, they learn intuitive physics, object permanence, gravity, causality. Most of human knowledge, and certainly almost all animal knowledge, has nothing to do with language.

That's why I keep saying we're not going to get to human-level intelligence just by scaling up LLMs trained on text. We need systems that learn world models from sensory input, things like video, and the way to do that, I think, is not with generative models that predict every pixel, but with architectures like JEPA, Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures, that make predictions in an abstract representation space. You learn a representation where the unpredictable details are eliminated, and you predict in that space. That's what will allow systems to reason, to plan, to have persistent memory, and to understand the physical world. And honestly, we don't have a machine that's as smart as a cat yet. That should tell you something about where the hard problem really is.

r001.rationale: It explains that language’s finite, discrete vocabulary makes next-word prediction tractable, communicating why it suits GPT-style prediction architectures.

r002.rationale: It explicitly describes the physical world as high-dimensional and contrasts that with language modeling.

r003.rationale: It explicitly describes the physical world as continuous and contrasts that with language modeling.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the thing people find surprising is that language is actually the easy part. Language is discrete. It's a sequence of tokens, a few tens of thousands of possible symbols, and at each step you're predicting a probability distribution over a finite set. That's a well-defined problem. You can never predict exactly which word comes next, but you can represent the uncertainty with a simple distribution, and the amount of information in text is small. A large language model is trained on roughly ten to the thirteen tokens, which sounds like a lot, but a four-year-old child has seen more data than that through their visual system alone in the first few years of life.

The physical world is continuous, high-dimensional, and noisy. If you try to do what LLMs do, which is predict the next frame of a video at the pixel level, you fail, because the world is only partially predictable. If I show you a video of this room and ask what happens next, you cannot predict where every pixel will be. There are infinitely many plausible futures, and you can't represent a distribution over them the way you can over words. So the system wastes all its capacity trying to predict details that are fundamentally unpredictable, and it learns nothing useful.

And yet a baby does this. By a few months old, infants have figured out that objects persist when hidden, that unsupported things fall, that one object can't pass through another. They learn intuitive physics by observation, without labels, without language, without anyone telling them Newton's laws. We don't know how to build a system that does that. Meanwhile we can build systems that pass the bar exam. That's the paradox, and it's basically Moravec's paradox again. The things that look intellectually impressive to us, like language and chess, are easy for machines, and the things any cat can do, like navigating a room and planning a jump onto a counter, are hard.

My view is that the way out is to predict in representation space rather than in input space. You learn an abstract representation of the world where the unpredictable details are discarded and only the predictable structure remains, and you make predictions there. That's what the JEPA architectures are about. The reason I say it's the harder problem is that solving it is what gets you to systems that can plan, that have common sense, that can reason about consequences of actions. Text alone doesn't give you that, because text is a very lossy, very compressed description of a world that the model has never actually observed.

r001.rationale: It describes language as the easy part for LLMs, emphasizing discrete tokens and next-token prediction over a finite set—language’s suitability for this model style.

r002.rationale: It says the physical world is high-dimensional, contrasting it with language as part of why world understanding is harder.

r003.rationale: It explicitly describes the physical world as continuous, contrasting it with discrete language.

astra-6.text:
Because language is already a very compressed, discrete description of the world. It leaves out an enormous amount of information that we take for granted. When I tell you that someone put a glass on a table, I don’t have to explain gravity, support, or what happens if you push the glass off the edge. You already have a model of those things. The words evoke that model; they don’t contain it.

Understanding the physical world means learning that underlying model from observation and interaction. You have to figure out what matters, how things evolve, and how your actions change them. And the world is only partially predictable. If you look at a tree blowing in the wind, you cannot predict the exact position of every leaf. But you can predict useful things about the tree. So the challenge is to learn representations that let you predict at the right level of abstraction, without having to predict every detail.

Animals do this remarkably well. A cat can navigate an unfamiliar room and plan a jump without language. That tells us there’s a powerful kind of intelligence underneath language that we haven’t yet reproduced adequately in machines. Producing fluent text is impressive, but it doesn’t, by itself, solve that problem.

r001.rationale: The response calls language a compressed, discrete description, but does not identify it as particularly well suited to GPT-style architectures.

r002.rationale: It mentions omitted information and unpredictable details such as leaf positions, but does not clearly attribute the difficulty to physical reality’s high dimensionality.

r003.rationale: It discusses how the physical world evolves, but does not state that its continuous nature makes it harder to understand.

sol-6.1.text:
Because language is already a very compressed, symbolic description of the world. When you describe an event in words, you leave out an enormous amount of detail. To understand the physical world, a system has to figure out which details matter, how things evolve, and what will happen if it takes an action.

Think about a video of a room. There are millions of pixels, but you don’t want to predict every pixel. You want to understand that there’s a table, that an object is resting on it, and that if you push the object beyond the edge, it will fall. The exact texture of the table is largely irrelevant. Learning that distinction, without someone labeling everything, is a very difficult problem.

And the world is only partially predictable. If I move an object behind another object, you can anticipate that it still exists, but you may not know precisely where it will reappear. So you need a model that captures the underlying structure and can handle uncertainty. Language gives you a lot of that structure already. With perception and action, the system has to discover it.

r001.rationale: The response says language is compressed and symbolic, but does not identify it as particularly well suited to GPT-style architectures.

r002.rationale: It cites the millions of pixels and enormous detail in video as part of why understanding the physical world is difficult.

r003.rationale: The response discusses physical change and uncertainty but does not attribute the difficulty to reality’s continuous nature.
